Q: How can I pull a model automatically with container creation? A:

This setup worked for me:

File docker-compose.yml

ollama:
  ...
  entrypoint: ["/entrypoint.sh"]
  volumes:
    - ...
    - ./entrypoint.sh:/entrypoint.sh
  ...

File entrypoint.sh

Make sure to run sudo chmod +x entrypoint.sh

Adapted from datawookie's script:

#!/bin/bash

# Start Ollama in the background.
/bin/ollama serve &
# Record Process ID.
pid=$!

# Pause for Ollama to start.
sleep 5

echo "Retrieving model (llama3.1)..."
ollama pull llama3.1
echo "Done."

# Wait for Ollama process to finish.
wait $pid

Why this approach?

By pulling the model in the entrypoint script rather than in the Docker image, you avoid large image sizes in your repository, storing the model in a volume instead for better efficiency.

Actually, when I think more about it, there might be scenarios where it’s worth putting the model into the image. Decide based on your use case.

Q: OpenAI Codex CLI isnt available on Windows yet, is there any other way i can have access to it? A:

I would set it up to run in the terminal using WSL2:

Install Node.js (≥22)

Codex CLI is a Node.js package, so you need Node 22 or later installed. Download from the official Node website and install it. Codex doesn’t run natively on Windows without a Linux-like environment, so you’ll want Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2) enabled. Most Codex users report it works best inside WSL2 rather than directly in PowerShell or CMD.

Open a terminal (WSL)

Launch your WSL2 distro (e.g., Ubuntu) so you’re inside a Linux environment. This avoids a bunch of quirks and bugs seen on native Windows terminals with Codex.

Install the Codex CLI

Run:

npm install -g @openai/codex

This installs the codex command globally so you can launch it from any folder.

Set your API key

You need to authenticate with OpenAI. Set your API key as an environment variable (replace with your key):

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-XXXX..."

If you want this automatically in every terminal session, add that line to your shell profile (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, etc.).

Run Codex

From your project folder:

codex

Q: Is it possible to run JavaFX applications in Java 8? A:

Java 8

At least two companies provide JDK/JRE products for Java 8 bundled with OpenJFX (the open-source implementation of JavaFX).

  • Azul Systems, with their JDK FX and JRE FX products, also known as ZuluFX.
  • BellSoft, with their LibericaFX products.

Several other vendors offer JDK/JRE products for Java 8. I do not know if any bundle OpenJFX. Vendors include: Amazon, IBM, Red Hat, Oracle, Adoptium of the Eclipse Foundation, SAP, Microsoft, and more.

Java 25

should be running in Java 25

Yes, if at all possible, you should be using later versions of Java and JavaFX (OpenJFX). Both have evolved greatly. You’ll enjoy the best performance, features, and support by using recent versions.

Generally I would recommend deploying to the latest LTS versions of both, which currently would be version 25. Then do your testing, and perhaps your development, with the latest version of both, which will be 26 next month. Releases of both Java and OpenJFX arrive every six months, March & September.

Bundling is optional

Using a JDK/JRE bundled with OpenJFX is one choice. Another is to add OpenJFX libraries to your project for use with a JDk/JRE from any of the vendors mentioned above.
